title: Overview: the big ideas
summary: The chapter's key concepts and how its sections fit together.

blocks.md: Welcome to **Model Training** (Vol I). This overview gives you the chapter's big ideas before the section-by-section lessons. Read the claims once, flip the flashcards, then take the warm-up quiz: it is fine to miss questions here, the lessons that follow fill the gaps.

Inference computes a forward pass as data flows through the network and a prediction emerges. Training adds a backward pass and an optimizer step, retains intermediate state, and repeats that work across many examples and optimization steps. Optimizers may also maintain momentum and variance estimates whose storage exceeds the model weights, so memory rather than arithmetic often decides what fits on a device.

nodes.label: From One Step to a Training Run
Computation and Memory Costs of Training

rows: **Training-time law**

In the macroscopic D·A·M product form of the iron law, training work is about 6PD FLOPs (D tokens times 6P FLOPs per token) and run time is that work over peak rate times utilization, so every point of utilization recovered at constant power removes time, energy, and dollars in the same proportion, while memory sits outside the law as a feasibility constraint.
**Model FLOPs utilization**

MFU is useful model FLOPs per step over peak times measured step time and is the honest estimate of utilization, whereas the busy time a device monitor reports is only an upper bound, high for a memory-stalled job and low for a data-starved one.
**Training memory at scale**

Mixed-precision Adam holds 16 bytes per parameter of static state (eight times the FP16 inference weights) before any activation, and only the activation term grows with batch and sequence length, which is what pushes a large model past one accelerator's memory.
**Mixed precision**

Running eligible matrix products in FP16 or BF16 raises the attainable peak and halves activation bytes but leaves the 16 B/param static state unchanged, FP16 needs dynamic loss scaling to keep gradients above its normal floor while BF16 usually does not, and the speedup is bounded by the work that stays off the matrix units.
**Checkpointing and accumulation**

Activation checkpointing recomputes segment interiors to cut activation memory from O(L) to O(sqrt L) for about one extra forward pass, and gradient accumulation builds a large effective batch from micro-batches that fit, reproducing the large-batch gradient only when losses are normalized consistently.
**Profile to find the limiting term**

Which technique helps depends on which resource is saturated, so the workflow is timeline first, then hardware counters, then one targeted fix and a re-profile, feasibility comes before speed, and a fix on a stage that is not the bottleneck buys nothing.
**Fine-tuning scope**

Training scope decides which memory terms exist: full fine-tuning of an 8B model needs about 128 GB of static state, while adapters such as LoRA shrink gradients and optimizer state to well under one percent of parameters, and activations still follow the backward path through every frozen layer.
**Training input pipeline**

Training throughput is the minimum of host preparation rate, host-link rate, and compute rate, and overlap makes the step cost the maximum of the stage times but cannot raise the slowest stage, so workers, prefetch depth, and pinned memory are sized against measured demand.
**IO-aware attention**

FlashAttention computes exact attention tile by tile in on-chip memory with online-softmax statistics and recomputes tiles in backward, dropping stored attention state from quadratic to linear in sequence length and cutting memory traffic without changing model FLOPs.
**Single-node data parallelism**

Data parallelism replicates the model and averages gradients with AllReduce, whose per-device traffic depends on parameter count rather than batch, so splitting a fixed batch across one node's accelerators raises the share of unhidden synchronization unless it overlaps with backward.
**Sharding within one node**

When per-replica state does not fit, ZeRO stages shard optimizer state, then gradients, then parameters across one node's accelerators, trading memory for communication, and layerwise model parallelism pays a pipeline bubble unless micro-batches are pipelined.
**Training checkpoints**

A training checkpoint saves persistent state (weights, master copy, optimizer moments) plus scheduler, RNG, data position, and scaler state for exact resume, and checkpoint cadence trades save stalls against replayed work, so fault tolerance is a throughput decision.
